en: The Jātaka,
Great Division (Mahānipāta), Chapter on the Mūgapakkha (The Dumb and Paralysed)
8. The Mahānāradakassapa Jātaka:
There was a king of the Videhas, a kshatriya named Aṅgati.
Abundantly endowed with yoga, wealthy,
and a man of infinite strength;
on the night of the fifteenth day, he—
In the first watch of the night, before dawn,
during the month of Kattika,
he summoned his ministers.
To the wise one, endowed with learning,
who was previously honored and possessed of insight—
to Vijaya and Sunāman—
To the general Alātaka,
the King of Videha questioned him:
"Speak each your own preference."
The four-month festival of the full moon has come,
its radiance dispelling the darkness; today,
my body delights in the night.
“Let us dwell in this season.
Then Senāpati Alāta spoke thus to the king:
“With all our strength, vigor, and power,
let us arm the army.
O King, lead us forth to battle!”
Possessing infinite strength and prowess,
those who do not come under our control—
we shall bring them under our sway.
“This is my own view;
we revere Ajita.
Having heard the words of Alāta, [he replied:]
We have heard this which he said:
“O Great King, all your enemies have come under your control.”
With weapons laid aside and enemies pacified,
we move toward a windless shelter;
today is the supreme festival.
War does not please me.
Let food, drink, and hard foods be quickly brought to you.
"O Rāma, gather the gods with sensual pleasures,
with dance, song, and beautiful music.
Having heard the words of Sunāma, [Rāma replied:]
Vijaya said this:
“O Great King, all sensual pleasures are constantly present for you.”
It is not difficult, O King,
to rejoice in sensual pleasures;
for sensual pleasures are always easily obtained.
This is not my considered view:
that we should attend upon a monk or a brahmin who is highly learned.
"O Sage who knows the meaning and the Dhamma, whoever has no doubt today regarding this Vinaya.
Having heard the words of Vijaya, [the Elder said:]
King Aṅgati said to me:
“Just as Vijaya speaks,
so too does this please me.”
Let us attend upon a recluse or even a brahmin who is very learned,
so that he may dispel our doubt today regarding the discipline.
The seers are knowers of the goal and the Dhamma.
All of you who are peaceful, form a consensus:
"Which wise man shall we attend upon?"
"Whoever has no doubt here regarding the Vinaya,
that sage is one who knows the meaning and the Dhamma.
Having heard the words of Vedeha, [he replied:]
Alāta said this:
"In this deer park, there is a naked ascetic who is esteemed as wise."
Guṇa, of the Kassapa clan,
is learned, an eloquent speaker,
and a leader of the assembly; O King, let us attend upon him.
“He will dispel my doubt.
Having heard Āḷāra’s words,
the king urged on his charioteer.
“We shall go to the Deer Park;
bring a suitable vehicle here.
They prepared his vehicle.
With ivory tusks like silver sheaths,
white with bright, polished rings, and a face as radiant as the moon.
There were four Sindhava horses yoked to it, adorned with white lotuses,
leaping like the wind.
Well-tamed, wearing golden garlands;
with a white parasol, a white chariot,
a white horse, and a white fan.
Vedeha, together with his ministers,
shines like the moon as he departs;
many followed after him.
Powerful heroes bearing swords on their fingers sat upon the backs of horses,
surrounding the lord of men, the best among men.
Having traveled for but a moment,
the Kṣatriya Vedeha alighted from his vehicle together with his ministers.
Pattī attained excellence.
And those brahmin women who were gathered there at that time, too—
King Apanayi did not remove him when he had reached the ground; then,
upon a soft mattress, he—
On a seat spread with soft cloth,
covered with a soft rug,
the king sat down to one side.
Having sat down, the king exchanged friendly greetings with him,
and then [asked]: "I hope, venerable sir, that you have what is needed for your sustenance?"
Are your humors not in discord?
Is your livelihood free from hardship?
Do you obtain enough almsfood to sustain yourself?
"Are you free from illness?
Does your sight not fail you?
Thus Guṇa greeted him in return.
“Vedeha, who delights in discipline:
‘All this, O Great King,
is merely for the sake of sustaining life.’”
I hope, O Vedeha, that the border regions do not grow too powerful;
I hope you are free from illness and fit for action.
Is your vehicle carrying you well?
Are there no diseases for you, and is your body free from affliction?
Having exchanged greetings, the king then immediately asked about welfare,
the Dhamma, and the right method.
The Bull among Charioteers, who loves the Dhamma, said:
“How, Kassapa, should a mortal practice the Dhamma toward his mother and father?”
How should one conduct oneself toward teachers?
How should one conduct oneself toward children and wives?
How should one conduct oneself toward the elderly?
How [should one behave] toward ascetics and brahmins?
And how should one conduct oneself among the army and in the countryside?
By practicing what kind of Dhamma do mortals go to a good destination?
And how is it that some remain established in non-Dhamma?
And they fall into hell.
Having heard these words of Vedeha,
Kassapa said this:
“Listen to me, O Great King,
the word that is true and not false:
there is no [obstacle] for one who practices the Dhamma.”
There is no fruit of good or evil deeds;
there is no other world, O King,
for who has ever come here from there?
There are no fathers, O King,
much less a mother or a father;
there is no such thing as a teacher.
Who will tame the untamed?
There are beings equal in strength,
with no one to show reverence to elders.
There is no power or vigor,
much less human effort or initiative;
for all beings are predetermined.
Just as with a cow that has been poisoned,
so it is for a mortal who obtains what he should not have obtained; how,
then, could there be the fruit of giving in that case?
There is no fruit of giving, O King;
one is powerless against the power of fate.
Giving was ordained only by fools.
Accepted by the wise,
fools who imagine themselves wise give their inheritance to the steadfast.
These seven eternal bodies are indestructible and unshakeable:
fire, earth, and water;
Wind, pleasure, and pain—
these seven bodies exist in living beings,
for which no cutter is found.
There is no slayer nor any cutter,
nor is there anyone who is slain;
it is only between the bodies [of aggregates] that...
Even one who, taking up a head with a sharpened blade,
[cuts it off] for others;
It does not cut that body;
how then could there be the fruit of evil therein?
For eighty-four great eons—
All are purified during the course of saṃsāra;
yet even one who is self-restrained is not purified when that time has not yet arrived.
Even having performed much that is auspicious,
they are not purified in the future;
and even having committed much evil, [they are not purified].
That moment does not pass us by.
Through gradual purification,
after eighty-four eons, we shall attain purity.
"One does not overstep destiny,
just as the ocean does not overstep its shore.
Having heard these words of Kassapa,
Alāta said this:
"Just as the venerable one says,
so it is pleasing to me as well."
I too remember my former birth as I wandered through existence;
I was named Piṅgala.
In the past, in the prosperous city of Benares, I was a hunter and a butcher of cattle;
much evil was committed by me there.
Many living beings were killed by me—
buffaloes, pigs, and goats.
Having passed away from there, I was born here.
Born into a family of powerful generals,
surely there is no evil fruit for me,
since I have not gone to hell.
Now at that time, there was a slave named Bījaka, a rag-picker;
while observing the Uposatha fast, he—
He approached Guṇasanti.
Having heard the words of Kassapa and the speech of Alāta, he [approached].
Sighing repeatedly and hotly,
he shed tears as he wept.
Vedeha questioned him:
“For what purpose do you weep, friend?
What have you heard or seen that makes you feel such pain?”
Having heard the words of Vedeha,
Bījaka said this:
“I have no painful feeling.”
Great King, listen to me:
I too remember my own former birth with happiness.
In the past, I lived in Sāketa as Bhāvaseṭṭhi,
devoted to virtuous qualities and esteemed by the brahmins.
Delighting in sharing and purity,
I do not recall having committed even a single evil deed myself.
Having passed away from there, O Vedeḥa,
I was born here in the womb of a wicked woman,
a slave-girl who carries water-jars.
Born thus into a miserable state, even while remaining in such misery,
he remained resolved upon a life of righteous conduct.
"I give half a portion of my food to whoever desires it,
on the fourteenth and the fifteenth day."
I always observe the fast-day vows;
I do not harm any living being,
and I avoid theft as well.
Indeed, it seems that all this well-practiced [virtue] is fruitless;
I consider this moral conduct to be useless.
Just as a firebrand appears to be burning,
so indeed do I grasp at the Kali age,
like a rogue who is not a thief.
He grasps the mat like a gambler learning his craft;
I do not see the door.
By which I shall go to a happy destination;
therefore, O King, I weep,
having heard the words spoken by Kassapa.”
Having heard the words of Bījaka,
King Aṅgati said:
“There is no gateway to a happy rebirth.”
O Bījaka, have confidence in destiny!
Whether it be happiness or suffering,
it is indeed through destiny that one obtains it.
Purification from saṃsāra comes to all;
do not be hasty regarding the future.
I too was virtuous in the past.
Engaged among the Brahmin women,
instructing them in their worldly affairs,
he was deprived of his delight in the meantime.
“Furthermore, venerable sir, we would like to see you,
if there is to be a meeting.
Having said this, the King of Videha—
He returned to his dwelling.
Then, at the end of the night,
he went to the assembly hall.
Having assembled his ministers,
he spoke these words:
"In my palace, Candaka..."
May they always grant me my desires;
may they not come upon me in matters of profit,
nor in those things that ought to be kept secret.
Vijaya and Sunāma,
and the general Alātaka—
let these sit upon this seat.
“...the three who are skilled in conventional usage.
Having said this, Vedeha [said],
“You think highly of sensual pleasures;”
Nor was he occupied with any purpose among the Brahmins. Then,
after seventeen nights had passed—
The daughter of the King of Videha was dear to him;
the princess named Rucā spoke to her nurse and mother.
“Adorn me quickly,
friends, and adorn me as well;
tomorrow is the divine fifteenth day.”
“I am going into the presence of the Lord.
To her, they brought garlands and highly precious sandalwood.
Jewels of gems, conch shells, pearls,
and various colorful garments,
as well as upon that golden throne—
Many women, surrounding her who was seated,
shone forth, she who was radiant and possessed of beautiful complexion.
And she, standing in the midst of her friends,
adorned with all her ornaments,
shone like the moon amidst the clouds.
He entered Cāndaka with splendor.
Having approached the Prince of Videha,
who delights in discipline, he paid homage to him.
He sat down to one side on a seat inlaid with gold.
And having seen him, the King of Videha—
Like the meeting of celestial nymphs,
he spoke these words to Rucā, who had come into the midst of her friends:
“Do you take delight in the palace,
gazing down at the lotus pond within?
Do you enjoy the many kinds of food?”
They always bring them.
Have the young maidens gathered many kinds of garlands?
Each member of the household prepares their own food,
constantly delighting in play and pleasure.
By what means, then, are you deficient?
"Bring them quickly!
O wall-faced one, make your mind as steady as the moon."
Having heard the words of Vedeha,
Ruci said to her father:
“All this, O Great King, is so.”
"It can be obtained from this person.
Tomorrow is the divine fifteenth day;
let them bring a thousand [pieces] to me."
"And as it was given, so shall I give;
I shall offer gifts to all who seek alms.
Having heard Rucā’s words, [he replied:]
King Aṅgati said to me:
"Much wealth has been wasted by you,
rendered useless and fruitless."
Since you always dwell on the Uposatha day and do not consume food or drink,
it is certain that this [body] must be left uneaten.
"There is no merit for one who does not eat.
For even a mere seed, having heard what was spoken by Kassapa at that time, [attained its fruit].
Sighing repeatedly with heat,
she wept and shed tears.
As long as she lived, she remained radiant.
"Do not take away my food!
There is no other world, O lady;
why do you distress yourself in vain?"
Having heard the words of Vedeha,
Rucā, of radiant complexion,
knowing the Dhamma in its prior and subsequent sequence, [spoke].
He said this to his father:
"This was indeed heard by me before,
but now it has been seen by me with my own eyes."
He who associates with fools becomes a fool himself;
for by approaching a fool,
the deluded one becomes deluded.
One falls into even greater delusion;
it is easy to be deceived by a firebrand or by a seed.
And you, O Lord, are wise,
steadfast, and skilled in the goal;
how could you be like fools?
He fell into a low view.
"If one is purified by the path of saṃsāra,
then renunciation is useless for the sake of virtue."
Like a moth plunging into a blazing fire,
he who is deluded by ignorance falls into nakedness.
Formerly, he was settled in the notion that "liberation comes through wandering."
Many fools, through ignorance, ruin their own karma;
like those who formerly grasped at a bad omen,
or like the fisherman with his hook, they are like the fish in the water.
I shall provide a simile for you,
O Great King, for your benefit;
for by means of a simile, some here [understand].
The wise understand the true purpose:
just as a ship belonging to merchants becomes heavy when overloaded with immeasurable cargo.
Having taken up an excessive burden,
one sinks in the ocean;
even so does a person who has committed evil.
Gathering even little by little,
yet taking up an excessive burden,
one sinks down into hell.
The burden is not yet full for the king who [takes] the ember,
and he continues to accumulate that evil.
By which one goes to a miserable destination—
his previously performed merit,
O Lord of the Earth, is like a spark.
O King, this is the very result of that:
whatever happiness he obtains,
his merit is being exhausted.
For thus he delights in what is devoid of virtue;
having abandoned the straight path,
he runs along a crooked path.
Just as when a balance is held steady and the weighing pans are set down,
it causes the head of the balance to rise.
When the burden has been laid down.
In the same way, a person who accumulates merit little by little;
One who is conceited about heaven is like a slave,
a seed-sower delighting in what is bitter.
That which is today a seed-sower and a slave—
He sees suffering within himself;
this is the evil he previously committed that he now experiences.
And his evil is destroyed,
for he delights in the Vinaya;
having attained the state of Kassapa, he is freed from all suffering.
Do not, O King, follow a wrong path. For whoever associates with another—
whether that person be virtuous or not— [he takes on their qualities].
Whether one is virtuous or immoral,
one comes under the influence of that very person;
for whatever kind of friend one makes, [so does one become].
As one associates with another,
so does one become;
for such indeed is the result of living together.
Serving one who serves,
and being touched by one who touches another,
like a poisoned arrow hitting a bundle of reeds—
What is not smeared becomes defiled; therefore,
out of fear of defilement, the wise person should never have evil friends.
The man who carries a putrid fish on the tip of a blade of kusa grass—
both the kusa grass and the fish give off a foul odor.
Such is the consequence of associating with fools: it is like a man who wraps up tagara incense in leaves.
Even the leaves emit a fragrant scent;
such is the service of the wise.
Therefore, just as with a leaf-bag, [one should associate with the virtuous].
Having understood this for himself,
the wise person should not associate with the wicked, but should associate with the virtuous.
The unwholesome lead to hell;
the wholesome cause one to reach a happy destination.
I too have passed through seven births.
All those who have wandered through existence,
as well as those yet to come— those seven types of beings whom I shall follow after passing away from here.
That which was my seventh birth,
O lord of men, in the past,
I was a smith’s son in Magadha.
In the past, in the city of Rājagaha,
having come upon an evil companion,
much evil was committed by me.
Harming another’s wife,
we wandered like immortals;
that deed, though set aside, [has come back to us].
Like a fire covered by ashes,
I was then born in Vaṃsabhūmi through other deeds.
In the city of Kosambī, O Great King, there was a merchant’s family—
prosperous, flourishing, and possessed of great wealth—
who had an only son.
Constantly honored and revered—
therein I would serve a friend,
a companion who delights in what is wholesome.
The wise one, endowed with learning,
established me in the goal on the fourteenth and fifteenth days.
I waited for many nights;
that deed, though set aside,
remained like a treasure near the water’s edge.
Now, as for this fruit of evil deeds that was committed by me in Magadha,
it has come upon me in its full measure later on.
Having become like a malignant poison,
O King of Videha, I fell from there and dwelt for a long time in the Roruva hell.
Because of my own karma, I am pursued;
I find no happiness in that place.
There, for many tens of millions of years,
Having endured much suffering,
O King, I became a goat with upturned testicles when my body was split open.
Sātaputtā was carried by me on my back and in my chariot;
this is the result of that deed.
Because of my going to another's wife,
O Vedeha, when I passed away from there,
I became a monkey in the great forest.
Just like a fruit plucked while still green by a reckless leader of the herd—
this is the result of that deed.
Because of my going to another's wife,
O Vedeḥa, having passed away from there,
I became a beast among those fit for sacrifice.
The noble steed has been stripped of its speed;
the harness has been worn by me for a long time.
This is the result of that deed.
Because of my going to another's wife,
O Vedeḥa, when I passed away from there,
I came to a family among the Vajjis.
I was neither female nor male when human existence was so very difficult to attain;
this is the result of that karma.
Because of my going to another's wife,
O Vedeḥa, when I passed away from there,
I was reborn in the Nandana grove.
In that palace,
I was a celestial nymph of beautiful form,
adorned with variegated garments and ornaments.
Wearing earrings of supreme jewels,
skilled in dance and song,
they were the attendants of Sakka.
Abiding there, O Videha,
I remember these births;
and those yet to come are likewise seven.
Whatever wholesome deed I have performed while at Kosambī shall follow me when I pass away from here.
I shall run on from here after death, among both gods and humans;
seven times of noble birth, O Great King.
Constantly honored and worshipped,
yet I shall not be released from womanhood—
these are the six miserable destinies.
And in my seventh rebirth, O Deva,
I shall be a son of the gods with great psychic power;
I shall become a male deity.
The supreme one among the host of gods;
even today, they weave this garland made of sandalwood in the Nandana grove.
A divine son named Java,
who accepts my garland;
that celestial being is like a mere moment.
Here, sixteen years are one divine day and night,
which is equal to a hundred human autumns.
Thus do karmas follow one through incalculable births,
whether they be wholesome or evil.
For indeed, karma does not perish.
Whatever man may wish to become,
birth after birth again and again—
One who desires to be a man should avoid another's wife, just as one with washed feet avoids the mud.
Birth after birth, again and again,
she should honor her husband as a handmaid honors Indra.
Whoever desires divine enjoyment,
divine lifespan, glory, and happiness,
should avoid all evil deeds.
One who is heedful and discerning should practice the Dhamma in three ways: by body, speech, and mind.
Whether it be a woman or a man, whatever these human beings in the world of the living may do for their own sake, [that they shall experience].
Those of great renown who possess all-encompassing wealth have,
without doubt, practiced virtue in the past;
for all beings alike are the owners of their own karma.
Come now, O Lord, reflect for yourself as well,
O King: what is the cause of these [visions] of yours,
which resemble celestial nymphs?
Thus, adorned and covered with a golden lattice,
the maiden Rucā gladdened her father Aṅgati.
She pointed out the path to the bewildered one and proclaimed the Dhamma, O lady of virtuous vows;
then she departed for the Brahma-world.
Nārada, surveying the human race in Jambudīpa,
beheld King Aṅgati.
Then, to the east of the palace of the King of Videha,
he saw that [palace] which had not yet been reached.
With joy, you paid homage to the Sage.
Then, descending from his seat,
the king was deeply distressed in mind.
Questioning Nārada,
he spoke these words:
"From where have you come, O one with the appearance of a god?"
Illuminating all directions like the moon,
being asked, tell me your name and clan,
and how people in the world of men know you.
“For I am now departing as a deity,
illuminating all directions like the moon;
being asked, I shall tell you my name and clan.”
“Nārada and Kassapa know me.
“Such as you are, of wondrous form,
you travel through the air and stand there;”
I ask you this matter, Nārada:
by what quality is this success of yours attained?
"Truth, Dhamma, self-control, and generosity..."
"These qualities were cultivated by me in the past;
through those very same well-practiced dharmas,
I have attained mental speed, by which I go wherever I desire."
“You proclaim a marvelous accomplishment of merit,
if indeed it is by these means as you say;
I ask you this matter, Nārada.”
“Being questioned by me, please explain it well.
“Ask me, O King, whatever matter you have,
whatever doubt you harbor, O protector of the earth.”
“I shall lead you to freedom from doubt by means of methods, principles,
and reasons. “I ask you this matter, Nārada:”
And being questioned by me, O Nārada, do not speak falsely:
"Are there gods? Are there ancestors?
Is there a world beyond, which people call the realm of Yama?"
“Indeed, there are gods and fathers;
there is another world, which they call the realm of men;
yet men are infatuated with sensual pleasures and utterly deluded.”
“Those possessed by delusion do not know the next world.
“If you believe, O Nārada,
that there is an abode for the dead in the next world;”
"Give me five hundred right here;
I will give you a thousand in the next world.
"I would indeed give five hundred to you, sir..."
If we could know that one who is virtuous and generous would dwell in hell while you, O cruel ones, remain there,
who in the next world would incite a thousand [to commit evil]?
Even here, the wise do not lend money to one who is unrighteous in character, of evil conduct, lazy, and cruel in his deeds.
For there is no tradition [of reproach] from such a person as that.
But when people have recognized a man who is capable,
industrious, virtuous, and generous;
They themselves will invite you to enjoy their wealth;
do not perform such deeds again.
When you have passed away from here, O King, you shall see that in the other world.
While dwelling in hell, being devoured by flocks of crows,
vultures, and hawks, he is being torn apart.
Who would urge one whose limbs are severed and from whom blood flows toward the world beyond?
Therein lies blinding darkness where neither moon nor sun shines.
Hell is always tumultuous and of a terrible form;
there, neither night nor day is discernible.
Who, seeking wealth, would wander about in such a place?
Sabala and Sāma, these two dogs,
with elongated bodies, powerful and great,
devour with their iron teeth.
Driven away from here and having reached the other world,
he dwells in hell, being devoured by gluttons,
beasts of prey, and the snakes of evil.
Who would urge one who has had their limbs severed and whose blood is flowing toward the world beyond with a thousand sharp spears and lances?
The black and dark-blue executioners strike and pierce the man who previously committed evil deeds in the terrible hell.
Being slaughtered and heading for hell,
with his belly ripped open in the womb,
his limbs severed and blood flowing—
Who would urge on such a person to the next world?
There, the gods rain down spears, arrows, lances, and slings, as well as various other weapons.
Flaming meteors fall like glowing coals;
stones rain down upon one who performs cruel deeds.
And the hot wind in hell is unbearable.
Not even for a moment can happiness be found therein;
who would urge such a person— who runs hither and thither,
afflicted by impurity— to the world beyond?
Even one who is running, yoked to chariots,
blazing with fire, treading upon the earth,
and being vigorously urged on by goads and staves—
Whoever would challenge another in the world beyond must ascend that mountain of razor-edged peaks—
terrifying, ablaze, and fearsome.
Who would urge one whose limbs are severed and from whom blood is flowing toward the next world— a thousand-fold [host]—
as he ascends that which resembles a mountain?
Who would incite another to a thousandfold torment in the next world— [to cast them] into a blazing, terrifying heap of burning coals, their limbs well-burnt, miserable, and weeping?
The trees are as high as water-tanks and covered with thorns;
they are [pierced] by sharp points made of iron.
Drinking human blood,
women ascend there,
as do men who have committed adultery with another's wife.
Driven by those with swords in hand who carry out the commands of Yama,
they ascend to that hell.
A *simbalī* tree smeared with blood,
its body scorched and its bark stripped away—
afflicted and in intense agony.
Exhaling repeatedly hot breaths,
a sinner for his past deeds,
with limbs like scorched wood on a mountain path.
Who would beg you for that wealth?
There are trees as high as mountain peaks,
covered with sword-leaves.
With sharp blades made of iron that drink the blood of men,
they [assail] him as he climbs that tree with sword-leaves.
Though being cut by sharp swords,
with limbs severed and blood flowing—
who would urge such a person toward the world beyond?
As soon as he has emerged from there,
he falls into the Vetaraṇī river, which is filled with trees whose leaves are swords.
Who would beg that wealth from you?
There is the river Vetaraṇī, difficult to cross, with rough, gritty, and scalding waters.
Covered with iron lotuses,
it flows with sharp blades;
there, its limbs are severed.
Who would beg you for that wealth as you are being carried away, smeared with blood, in the supportless Vetaraṇī?
“I am being pierced as if a tree were being cut down;
I do not know the directions, my consciousness is utterly bewildered.
I am filled with fear and remorse, for my terror is great.”
Having heard these words spoken by you,
these people are like those who have entered the midst of water where it is ablaze,
or like an island in a great ocean of floodwaters.
Like a lamp in the darkness,
you are our refuge, O Lord.
Teach me the goal and the Dhamma, O Lord.
"I have committed offenses in the past;
tell me the path of purity, O Nārada,
so that I may not fall into hell."
“As Dhatarattha was,
so were Vessamitta, Aṭṭhaka, Yamataggi,
Usindara, and King Sivi.”
These were the attendants of the ascetics and brahmins—
these and other kings who have gone to the heavenly realm.
Avoiding what is unrighteous,
O lord of the earth, practice what is righteous;
and let those with food in their hands [wait] for you in the open air.
Let it be proclaimed throughout your city:
"Who is hungry? Who is thirsty?
Who needs garlands? Who needs ointment?"
Who, being naked, will put on garments of various colors?
And who carries an umbrella along the road?
"And sandals soft and beautiful—
let these be proclaimed throughout your city, both evening and morning."
Do not employ as before an aged ox or horse;
you should instead provide them with maintenance.
That which is determined by one's spiritual authority is powerful: "Your body is known as a chariot,
with the mind as its swift charioteer."
Non-violence as its spokes,
sharing as its fender, mindfulness as its wheels,
and self-restraint as its hub.
Restrained in his hands,
moderate in his belly, restrained in his speech,
and not making a sound.
With limbs perfected by truthful speech,
well-restrained from slander,
and with his voice free from harshness and crookedness;
Measured in speech, firm in resolve,
well-prepared through faith and diligence,
with palms joined in reverence like a hollowed bowl.
Free from dullness and over-zeal,
bound by the restraint of virtue,
unangry and not given to violence—
The Dharma is the white umbrella;
great learning is the handle,
and the settled mind is the frame.
The heart-essence is knowledge of the right time,
the staff is the possession of self-confidence,
and the upper garment is humble conduct.
The age of non-conceit is swift;
with a mind free from dejection,
serving those who have grown great, one is cleansed of dust.
Mindfulness is the goad of the wise man;
fortitude and application are his reins.
The tamed mind leads him along the path.
With even teeth and steady gait;
desire and greed are the wrong path,
while self-restraint is the straight path.
O King, wisdom is the goad for forms, sounds, tastes, smells, and for a galloping horse.
In this regard, the self is the charioteer.
If, by means of this vehicle,
one possesses firm conduct and steadfastness;
“O King, you are a granter of all desires;
you shall never fall into hell.
“Alāta, you are Devadatta!”
Sunāma was Bhaddaji;
Vijaya was Sāriputta,
and Bījaka was Moggallāna.
Sunakkhatta, son of the Licchavis,
was once a naked ascetic (acelaka);
Ānanda was then Ruci.
She who had inspired confidence in the king— Uruvelakassapa,
at that time, held an evil view.
"The Bodhisatta was Mahābrahmā;
thus you should remember this Jātaka.
Thus ends the eighth Jātaka, the Mahānāradakassapa Jātaka.
